conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.message: Let's work on the House Robber problem. You're a robber planning to rob houses along a street. Each house has money, but you can't rob adjacent houses or the alarm will go off. What's the maximum money you can rob?

conversation.speaker: candidate
conversation.message: Okay, so I can't rob houses next to each other. Let me think... maybe I could try all possible combinations?

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.message: That's one approach. Can you think about what the choice is at each house?

conversation.speaker: candidate
conversation.message: Um, at each house I can either rob it or not rob it?

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.message: Exactly! And if you rob house i, what constraint does that put on house i-1?

conversation.speaker: candidate
conversation.message: If I rob house i, then I can't rob house i-1. So I can only get money from house i plus whatever I got from houses before i-1?

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.message: Great! So if you rob house i, you get nums[i] + (best result from houses 0 to i-2). What if you don't rob house i?

conversation.speaker: candidate
conversation.message: If I don't rob house i, then I just get the best result from houses 0 to i-1?

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.message: Perfect! So at each house, you take the maximum of these two choices. Does this remind you of any algorithmic technique?

conversation.speaker: candidate
conversation.message: Hmm... it sounds like I'm building up the solution from smaller problems? Is this dynamic programming?

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.message: Exactly! You're breaking the problem into subproblems. Can you define what dp[i] would represent?

conversation.speaker: candidate
conversation.message: dp[i] would be... the maximum money I can rob from houses 0 to i?

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.message: Yes! And what would be the recurrence relation based on our discussion?

conversation.speaker: candidate
conversation.message: dp[i] = max(dp[i-1], nums[i] + dp[i-2])? Because I either don't rob house i and take dp[i-1], or I rob house i and add it to dp[i-2]?

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.message: Excellent! You've got the recurrence relation. What about base cases?

conversation.speaker: candidate
conversation.message: For base cases... dp[0] would be nums[0] since there's only one house. And dp[1] would be max(nums[0], nums[1]) since I pick the better of the first two houses?

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.message: Perfect reasoning! Now can you try to implement this?

conversation.speaker: candidate
conversation.message:
Let me try... 
```python
def rob(nums):
    if len(nums) == 1:
        return nums[0]
    
    dp = [0] * len(nums)
    dp[0] = nums[0]
    dp[1] = max(nums[0], nums[1])
    
    for i in range(2, len(nums)):
        dp[i] = max(dp[i-1], nums[i] + dp[i-2])
    
    return dp[-1]
```

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.message: Great implementation! Let's trace through an example. What happens with [2,7,9,3,1]?

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.message: Perfect trace! You robbed houses with values 2, 9, and 1 for a total of 12. What's the time and space complexity?

conversation.speaker: candidate
conversation.message: Time complexity is O(n) because I go through the array once. Space complexity is O(n) for the dp array?

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.message: Correct! Can you think of how to optimize the space complexity? Notice that you only need the previous two values.

conversation.speaker: candidate
conversation.message: Oh! Instead of keeping the whole array, I could just keep two variables for the previous two results and update them as I go?

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.message: Exactly! That would make it O(1) space. You've shown great learning ability and worked through this systematically. Well done!
